item.title: “Wake-up call” after alcohol-related traffic deaths increase
item.description:
“Wake-up call” after alcohol-related traffic deaths increase

November 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

As many as one-third of traffic deaths in the Netherlands involve a driver who was under the influence of alcohol, according to a new study by road safety research bureau SWOV.

Researchers estimate that 180 and 270 people died in collisions where alcohol was a factor, representing between 24% and 35% of all deaths. In one-third of cases the victim was not the driver of the vehicle.

The figures suggest the proportion of alcohol-related deaths is increasing. In the last analysis in 2013 SWOV calculated that between 19% and 28% of road deaths were the result of drink-driving.

At the same time the total number of deaths on the roads has been rising since 2022, after a steady decline between the 1970s and 2010. Last year 759 people died in traffic collisions, the highest number since 2007.

37% of victims were cyclists, 30% were drivers or passengers in vehicles and 8% were on foot. The rest were travelling on motorbikes, mopeds and scooters, or in lorries.

The latest estimates by SWOV also show a rise in the number of people admitted to hospital with injuries sustained in alcohol-related collisions. In 2025 between one-sixth and a quarter of admissions were alcohol-related, compared to up to one-fifth in 2013.

The figures are estimates because Dutch law prevents testing being carried out on the bodies of people who die in traffic collisions, even if they are suspected of drink-driving, because they cannot be prosecuted.

Wake-up call

SWOV researcher Heike Martensen said the figures were “shocking” and a “wake-up call” for politicians and the justice system.

She said more effort needed to be put in to detecting drink-drivers after SWOV found that the proportion of all drivers who had consumed alcohol had risen from 1.7% to 2.3%.

Police have cut back on large-scale roadside breath tests because drivers can use social media to alert each other to their presence, which has reduced their visibility, Martensen told Dutch News.

“The chance of being caught hasn’t gone down, but people’s perception is that the risk is lower,” she said. “If people think the chance is small, the consequences are less effective.”

Alcohol locks

Martensen also called for the government to review direct sanctions such as fitting alcohol locks on cars of people who have been convicted of drink-driving, so that they have to pass a breath test before they can start the engine.

An earlier scheme to enforce the device through court orders was abandoned 10 years ago after judges said it amounted to a “double punishment”. The court also said the high cost of fitting a lock for two years were too punitive for offenders who were unable to afford them.

Martensen said advances in car technology had brought the cost down to the point where all new cars could potentially have the option of fitting an alcohol lock.

“We think it should be re-evaluated. We know from other countries that it is an effective way of preventing people driving under the influence of alcohol.”

Awareness not enough

Fitting alcohol locks as standard on all cars would be the ultimate step, but Martensen admitted that there was no public support for such a move at the moment.

“Look at seatbelts – that problem was solved when cars forced people to wear them,” she said. “Hardly anybody drives without a seatbelt now, so if the car forced you to drive sober it would solve the problem.”

She said awareness campaigns were not enough on their own to change people’s drinking and driving habits. “It’s part of a wider social problem. People who repeatedly drive under the influence often have issues with alcohol addiction,” she said.

“And then you have situations where people have a drink and don’t have any other means of getting home. Having alternative options like public transport is more effective than telling people it’s dangerous to drink and drive.”

item.title: DNB warns AI, cyberattacks and debt could rock financial system
item.description:
DNB warns AI, cyberattacks and debt could rock financial system

November 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch central bank DNB has issued a new warning that a convergence of risks is posing a severe threat to the country’s financial stability; namely, the power of AI cyberattacks, the possibility of an AI economic bubble, and the fact that only a small number of cybersecurity companies are protecting financial institutions.

At the same time, interest rate rises are putting increasing pressure on government debt.

“The systemic risk lies primarily in the potentially dangerous confluence of shocks, such as cyberattacks, a stock market correction, or the impact of higher interest rates,” DNB president Olaf Sleijpen said in a statement on Tuesday.

“Moreover, the ability to absorb setbacks has diminished now that government fiscal space is limited. As a result, shocks can spread more quickly and widely throughout the financial system.”

There is widespread fear that massive global investments in AI infrastructure could cause an economic downturn. The DNB notes that the Dutch investment exposure here is around €13.5 billion (compared with global AI investment of around $1 trillion this year, according to Goldman Sachs).

While this amount is relatively limited, complex financial structures and the use of leverage (borrowing money to fund investments, which amplifies gains and losses) mean impacts can spread fast and are hard to predict.

Interest rates around the world have risen sharply in recent months, to their highest level since 2000, DNB said. That makes it more expensive for governments to borrow, and harder for countries that are already deep in debt to pay it off.

Governments also have less money to spare for a new crisis than they did during the coronavirus pandemic, the bank said.

DNB said banks, insurers and pension funds should keep investing in protection against cyberattacks and in back-up systems. They should also hold regular crisis drills with other key sectors such as energy and telecoms.

It also called for better crisis planning across Europe and closer ties between EU banking and investment markets, so companies can make more of opportunities such as AI. That, the bank said, will take “political will and courage”.

item.title: MPs vote to remove “remigration” from language of Dutch law
item.description:
MPs vote to remove “remigration” from language of Dutch law

November 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch MPs have voted to change the name of the Remigration Act to a more neutral term amid warnings that the term has become a rallying cry for far-right groups.

The law was passed in 1999 to allow benefits to be paid to migrants who return to their country of origin voluntarily, but no claims have been processed since the start of last year.

The English term is widely used on government websites such as the social security bank (SVB) that advise Dutch residents on how to claim benefits.

Security services have warned that “remigration” is increasingly by far-right political parties as a euphemism for enforced deportation.

“If extremist ideas and language are normalised and the boundaries shift, it can have implications for people’s safety,” the intelligence agency AIVD and anti-terrorism co-ordinator NCTV warned in a recent report.

The three coalition parties D66, VVD and CDA supported a motion by the left-wing opposition party Pro on Tuesday that would remove the word “remigration” from the name and text of the 1999 law.

Payments to Syrians

The right-wing party JA21 and independent MP Mona Keijzer tabled a motion calling for the government to start funding the payments again so the law could be reactivated, but the plan was voted down.

The VVD succeeded with a motion to offer Syrians a one-off payment of €10,000 to leave the country if they agree to return home voluntarily.

The government says large areas of Syria are safe to return to, even though the Dutch embassy in Damascus remains closed and the official travel advice says it is “too dangerous“ for visitors because of the “unpredictable” situation.

Parliament also passed a motion by the far-right PVV which would allow dual nationals to have their Dutch passport cancelled if they join proscribed organisations such as Al Qaida or Islamic State.

item.title: Prosecutors demand life sentence for Tarwekamp mastermind
item.description:
Prosecutors demand life sentence for Tarwekamp mastermind

November 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prosecutors have called for a life sentence for the man accused of masterminding the Tarwekamp explosion in The Hague in 2024, which killed six people and collapsed a part of an apartment complex.

The public prosecution service (OM) told the district court on Tuesday that the defendant, Moshtag B., came up with the “insane plan” as revenge against his ex-girlfriend. He sought to blow up the bridal shop she ran on the ground floor of the building, it said.

The OM wants 30 years for Mourad ben T. (31), who they say carried out the attack, and 28 years for his cousin Ilias B. (31), who took part but didn’t come up with the plan. Adil A. (34) faces a possible four-year sentence because he was involved in the plan but pulled out beforehand.

According to the OM, the attack was planned for months in advance. The men allegedly looked up how flammable wedding dresses were and worked out in a group chat how to best burn the shop down. On the day, they used high-powered fireworks and around 175 litres of petrol.

The blast hit the Mariahoeve district at around 6.15am on December 7, 2024. Besides the six who were killed, it also injured five people and left a row of homes in ruins.

Three of the six people who died were from one family: a father (45), a mother (41) and their 17-year-old daughter. Their 8-year-old son was the only one of them pulled alive from the rubble. The others killed were two men aged 44 and 63, who also lived on the Tarwekamp, and a 31-year-old man from Voorburg who was staying with a friend in the building.

Within a fortnight, B. had been identified as the ex-partner of the shop’s owner. Broadcaster NOS reported that he was in London when the explosion happened.

At a pre-trial hearing in March last year, B. told judges he was “so unbelievably sorry”.

NOS said the four men barely reacted when the sentences were read out. Victims’ relatives were split: many thought the demands were tough, but some had hoped for heavier ones.

item.title: Amsterdam poverty rate double the national average, CBS says
item.description:
Amsterdam poverty rate double the national average, CBS says

November 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam has the highest share of people living in poverty in any of the major cities in the Netherlands, according to new figures from national statistics office CBS, which also show over half a million people are below the bread line.

Some 6% of Amsterdam residents were classed as poor in 2025, double the national rate of 3%. The national figure was unchanged on 2024. The Hague (5.9%) and Rotterdam (5.6%) were close behind.

The CBS counts someone as poor if they do not have enough left to live on after paying fixed costs such as rent, energy and health insurance. Nationwide, 521,000 people fell below the line.

Only Vaals in Limburg had a higher rate than Amsterdam, at 6.4%. Tubbergen in Overijssel had the lowest, at 0.9%.

When Amsterdam first had the biggest share of poverty among big cities, its then poverty chief Marjolein Moorman said the figures ignore local support such as the Stadspas discount card and free laptops, Het Parool reported.

CBS economist Peter Hein van Mulligen told the paper that was possible, but that the effect is unknown because some other councils have similar schemes.

The figures more people might be missing out on that help. A third of people in poverty nationwide now live mainly on income from work.

Poverty among workers rose from 1.9% to 2.1%, driven by the self-employed. Freelancers (zzp’ers) without staff have a poverty rate of 4.3%, compared with 1.7% for employees.

“People with a job who live below the poverty line are often invisible to the council,” Van Mulligen told Het Parool.

item.title: Bosz says PSV were “trampled” after Real hit five in second half
item.description:
Bosz says PSV were “trampled” after Real hit five in second half

November 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

PSV and Feyenoord face an uphill task to reach the group stages of the Champions League after defeats on Tuesday night saw them drop out of the qualifying places.

PSV briefly threatened to cause an upset in Madrid as they took a 1-0 lead into the half-time break. Ivan Perisic’s penalty after 32 minutes was their only reward for a courageous first-half display in which Ruben van Bommel and Sven Mijnans also missed clear chances to score.

But the introduction of Jude Bellingham at half-time changed the picture as Real’s superstars regrouped to score five goals. The England midfielder’s dazzling volley was the pick of the bunch, while Kylian Mbappé bagged a double and Vinicius Junior also got on the scoresheet.

Head coach Peter Bosz admitted his team had been “trampled underfoot” in the second half. “I think you had to be there to see how big the difference was between the first and second half,” he said.

“In the first half we were brave, put our opponents under pressure and had three big chances in the first four minutes.

“When you look at the second half, they scored quickly and the tempo of their game was much higher. That’s the quality they have with the players they can bring off the bench.”

Feyenoord beaten

PSV’s next match is a home tie against Real’s city rivals Atletico on December 9, before they travel to Stavanger to take on Viking in January and round off the group stage at home to Stuttgart.

Feyenoord suffered a narrower defeat at home to Porto as they were unable to recover from an own goal after two minutes by Oussama Targhalline.

Goalkeeper Florian Kastenmeier vindicated the decision of Giovanni van Bronckhorst to replace the out-of-form Tjark Ernst by making some vital saves to keep the Rotterdammers in the game.

Feyenoord staged a late rally, with Gjivai Zechiël going close and Targhalline striking the crossbar from long range, but they were unable to breach the Portuguese side’s defence.

The fans in De Kuip were briefly celebrating after a bizarre incident when referee Irfan Peltjo’s watch told him a header by Nacho Ferri had crossed the line, but video replays clearly showed it bounced off the post and into the hands of Diogo Costa.

Feyenoord have just three points from their five matches so far, one less than PSV. Their next two matches are away to Viking on December 8 and Galatasaray on January 19, before they close their campaign in Rotterdam against RB Leipzig.

item.title: Appeal court rejects state bid to pause Bonaire climate ruling
item.description:
Appeal court rejects state bid to pause Bonaire climate ruling

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands has to draft binding national targets, the Court of Appeal in The Hague has ruled, after the state requested a suspension of its obligation.

The ruling is another step in the Bonaire climate case, which was taken to court by Greenpeace on behalf of the residents of the Dutch island in the Caribbean, where climate change is destroying the coral reef.

That case was won in January, and the court found that the government in The Hague had acted in a discriminatory manner to its people there.

Part of the ruling was that the Netherlands must set binding emissions targets for the whole economy in law by July 28, 2027, as well as draw up an adaptation plan for Bonaire that can be implemented by 2030. The ruling must be carried out even while an appeal is under way.

The government appealed the ruling in April, requesting a suspension. The Court of Appeal has largely rejected that request, but said international air and maritime transport can be left out of the targets but the government must move otherwise forward.

Marieke Vellekoop, director of Greenpeace Netherlands, said in a reaction: “The state has once again been reminded of its responsibility. Executing the judgment is not a non-binding ambition, but an obligation.”

Vellekoop said it was “incomprehensible that the state is doing everything it can to delay climate action,” while the consequences of the climate crisis are becoming increasingly severe. “On Bonaire, but also here in Europe. The cabinet must stop delaying and get to work now.”

item.title: Erasmus MC head of intensive care steps down over safety report
item.description:
Erasmus MC head of intensive care steps down over safety report

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The head of intensive care at Rotterdam’s Erasmus Medical Centre, Diederik Gommers, has stepped down in the wake of a damning report into a “culture of fear” that potentially compromised the safety of staff and patients.

The healthcare inspectorate IGJ said the situation in the department, the largest in the Netherlands, amounted to “a serious threat to the safety of patients or care”.

Gommers, who became one of the public faces of the Netherlands’ coronavirus response in 2020 when he was a member of the government’s Outbreak Management Team, quit his post with immediate effect when the findings became known this week.

The department’s board of directors has been placed under heightened supervision after the report said the psychological safety of staff was compromised by a management that did not accept being challenged or criticised.

The Erasmus MC hospital said in a statement on its website that it accepted it should have recognised the warning signs and taken action sooner.

“We are sorry that some colleagues did not feel safe enough to voice their concerns. Everyone should feel free to express their views, challenge each other and share signs.”

The hospital added that there was no suggestion patients had received substandard care as a result of the problems in the department.

18-month investigation

Inspectors began investigating the ICU 18 months ago after a whistleblower raised concerns about the workplace culture.

NOS late-night news show Nieuwsuur and regional news channel Rijnmond said they had seen hundreds of internal emails and documents going back five years and spoken to 26 current and former staff about the situation.

Doctors said “tensions” between medical specialists deterred staff from speaking out if they were critical of or worried about their colleagues’ decisions.

Jan Maarten van den Berg, a former healthcare inspector who specialised in intensive care, told Nieuwsuur: “These conclusions are very severe. There needs to be a breakthrough in the situation at Erasmus for the sake of the patients.”

Nieuwsuur earlier reported that Gommers did not have the legally required qualifications to carry out medical research on patients. The hospital said Gommers had not done any clinical research since 2023 and had started studying to obtain his certificates.

item.title: Juice and milk bottles to join deposit scheme in 2027
item.description:
Juice and milk bottles to join deposit scheme in 2027

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch packaging trade association Verpact has announced it will begin a deposit return system for plastic juice and dairy bottles on its own initiative, according to broadcaster NOS.

Plastic juice and dairy bottles of up to three litres will carry a deposit (statiegeld) from next year. Verpact said it is preparing a phased rollout in 2027. Labels, return machines, IT systems and logistics will all have to be adjusted.

The move follows pressure from climate and green growth minister Stientje van Veldhoven, who wants 90% of plastic bottles sold in the Netherlands to be collected by January 1, 2028. According to NOS, that target cannot be met without juice and dairy bottles.

In September, Van Veldhoven proposed making deposits compulsory on all plastic bottles up to three litres and banning the sale of bottles and cans without a deposit.

Dairy bottles have so far been exempt because producers say they are hard to clean, and the minister has made hygiene measures a condition. Many juice producers already charge a deposit voluntarily.

item.title: Cold comfort: Dutch skater smashes one-hour natural ice record
item.description:
Cold comfort: Dutch skater smashes one-hour natural ice record

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Marathon skater Judith Krabbenborg has taken advantage of the early cold snap to smash the world one-hour record for skating on natural ice.

The 29-year-old took to the ice in Winterswijk, Gelderland, at 8.30am on Tuesday and covered a distance of 34 kilometres 878 metres, beating the previous women’s record by 2.6 kilometres.

“I could feel my legs and my back hurting at the end, but there were so many people standing on the sidelines that it gave me energy,” she told NOS.

The previous record, set four years ago by Femke Mossinkoff, also in Winterswijk, was the first official time for the hour by a woman on natural ice. On the same day Bart Vreugdenhil set the current men’s record of 36 kilometers 717 metres.

Most skating records are set on artificial ice, but Winterswijk is one of three arenas where the local club has been able to create a natural arena for early-morning skaters during the recent cold weather.

The all-time women’s record is 40 kilometres 569 metres, set by another Dutch skater, Carien Kleibeuker, in Inzell, Austria, in 2015.

The rink at Winterswijk closed a few hours after Krabbenborg’s record-breaking skate as the ice started to melt, but it is expected to be available again on Wednesday morning.
